attribution.note: This is a section headline Zitron wrote in his own post. The 80% figure is his reading of Ramp's data, presented as his own assertion.

semantics.note: The proposition matches the headline. It combines a revenue-share observation with a causal 'pump' assertion. The body is narrower than the headline: it says 80% comes from 1% of customers, most of them VC-backed.

contract.note: Reading the 80% per provider and using the July–September 2026 window are evaluator choices, but both are ordinary readings. No evidence settles either component under any reasonable reading, so interpretation does not decide the result.

evidence.note: Ramp reports that 1% of firms drive 80% of combined OpenAI/Anthropic spend. It gives no venture-funding split, no separate figure for each provider, and no period, so it cannot establish the VC-backed share.
Company page on discounted prepaid bundles for Pro/Max/Team plans. It covers a different product scope and gives no measured revenue effect, so it does not show enterprise discounts boosting revenue.

reviews.rationale: Neither component is settled. No source splits either provider's enterprise revenue by venture-funding status: Ramp measures spending concentration, not VC backing. No evidence measures incremental revenue from Anthropic's enterprise discounts. Nothing in the packet contradicts the claim either.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence, concluding his own calculation.

semantics.note: 'Guaranteed to be a fraction of the real number' means the true share exceeds his lower-bound estimate of nearly one-quarter. The proposition captures this.

contract.note: It is fair to compare against his own minimum (4.59/19.708) for the June 2026 TTM period. Flagging the arithmetic mismatch and possible overlap between brackets is appropriate. Excluding accounts receivable as a proxy for revenue is reasonable.

evidence.note: The S-1 gives top-five customers at ~25% of revenue for January–September 2026, and its customer thresholds are on a September TTM basis. Both are different periods from the June TTM claim, so the filing does not settle the June share.

reviews.rationale: Nothing in the packet gives the June 2026 TTM revenue from the large-customer groups. The filing's concentration data cover other periods, and receivables are not revenue. The claimed lower bound can be neither confirmed nor refuted.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. The hedged aside about Anthropic's IPO ('I believe') is correctly left out; the claim covers only the Meta assertions.

semantics.note: Factual parts ($97.5B ATM, dilution, slowing Muse growth) are mixed with evaluative or rhetorical parts ('little or no AI strategy', 'cons retail'). The proposition keeps all of them.

contract.note: Reading 'collapsing growth' as a sharp slowdown in user additions is charitable and ordinary. Requiring evidence of misleading disclosures for 'cons retail' is fair. Treating 'at-the-market' as a checkable label decides the financing component.

evidence.note: Meta's own offering terms put ATM capacity at up to $60B, starting in Q1 2027. That contradicts calling it a $97.5B ATM program.
The underwritten offerings ($25B common plus $12.5B preferred) and the $60B ATM sum to $97.5B. The headline figure is the whole package, not the ATM.
Daily-active-user additions slowed about 62% from the launch surge through October 6, while users still grew. This supports sharply slowing growth. The publisher's affiliate held a short position.

reviews.rationale: The $97.5B total is right, but calling it an at-the-market offering is wrong: the ATM is $60B and has not started. Sharply slowing Muse user growth is supported. Completed dilution, 'little or no AI strategy', and 'cons retail' are not established and are largely evaluative.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sentence. It follows his quotation of The Information's Replit report.

semantics.note: He links the minimum-spend demands to either alienating customers or draining their funding. 'Dangerous game' is rhetorical framing around a checkable causal core. 'Some of' is kept.

contract.note: Reading the claim as material commercial harm, with the two outcomes as alternatives, is fair and not stretched. It does not require an unavoidable binary outcome. The result depends on accepting the alienation branch.

evidence.note: A secondhand summary of The Information: Replit moved most spending to OpenAI after Anthropic tied its discount to a larger commitment. The source is anonymous and TNW says it has not verified it.
Replit's CEO says Replit was a top-five customer and switched for cost, partnership, and performance. This corroborates the shift and cost as one factor. Insiders dispute that the partnership ended.

reviews.rationale: A former top-five customer, Replit, moved its default and most of its spending to OpenAI. Reporting ties this to Anthropic requiring a larger spending commitment to keep a discount, and the CEO cites cost among his reasons. That meets the contract's alienation branch. The causal link rests on anonymous, secondhand reporting, and the funding-drain branch is not shown.
